subject: chemistry
title: Required practical: making a soluble salt
key_idea: To make a pure, dry soluble salt from an acid and an insoluble solid, add the solid to the acid until it is in excess, filter, then crystallise the filtrate. If the reactant is soluble, find the exact volumes by titration, then repeat without the indicator.

blocks.text: Soluble salts can be made from an acid and a solid insoluble in water: a metal, metal oxide, metal hydroxide or metal carbonate.

items: The acid gives the type of salt: chlorides from hydrochloric acid, nitrates from nitric acid, sulfates from sulfuric acid.
With copper oxide, the black powder disappears and the mixture turns blue.
With copper carbonate, the green solid disappears, the mixture fizzes and a blue solution forms.

blocks.label: Copper oxide with sulfuric acid
blocks.formula: copper oxide + sulfuric acid → copper sulfate + water

blocks.label: Copper carbonate with sulfuric acid
blocks.formula: copper carbonate + sulfuric acid → copper sulfate + water + carbon dioxide

items.meaning: More of a reactant than is needed, so some is left over when the reaction stops.
The solution that passes through the filter paper.
Forming solid crystals from a solution, by evaporating some of the water and cooling.

items: Use an acid and an insoluble metal, oxide, hydroxide or carbonate.
The acid decides whether the salt is a chloride, nitrate or sulfate.

sections.heading: The method and the reason for each step

blocks.text: This is the method for pure, dry copper sulfate crystals from copper oxide and sulfuric acid. It works for any insoluble solid.

diagram.alt: Put the steps for making copper sulfate crystals in order.
diagram.prompt: Put the method for making pure, dry copper sulfate crystals in order
steps: Warm the dilute sulfuric acid in a beaker
Add copper oxide a spatula at a time, stirring
Stop when some copper oxide is left over
Filter off the excess copper oxide
Heat the filtrate in an evaporating basin until crystals start to form
Leave the solution to cool and crystallise
Pat the crystals dry with filter paper

items.text: Use a Bunsen burner or a water bath. This speeds up the reaction.
Keep adding until some solid remains. For a carbonate, there is also no more fizzing.
This removes the excess solid. The filtrate is only salt and water.
Heat the filtrate gently in an evaporating basin, on a water bath or electric heater, until crystals start to form. Do not heat to dryness.
Leave the solution to cool so crystals grow.
Pat the crystals dry between filter papers, or leave them in a warm place.

items: Add excess solid so all the acid reacts.
Filter to remove the excess, then evaporate part of the water and leave to crystallise.

sections.heading: When the reactant is soluble: titration

blocks.text: Soluble alkalis such as sodium hydroxide, potassium hydroxide and ammonia solution cannot be added in excess and filtered off. Titration is used instead.

diagram.alt: Comparing making a salt from an insoluble solid and from a soluble alkali.

rows.feature: How to know the acid is used up
values: Indicator changes colour in a titration
No excess: use the exact volumes found

items: Titrate the acid with the alkali, using an indicator, to find the volumes that react exactly.
Mix the same volumes again in the correct proportions, **without the indicator**. An indicator would contaminate the salt.
The solution left is only salt and water.
Evaporate to concentrate the solution, leave to cool and crystallise, then dry the crystals.
A pH probe can be used instead of an indicator. It does not contaminate the solution.
A soluble reactant cannot be filtered off, so a titration finds the exact volumes.
Repeat with the same volumes and no indicator, so the salt is pure.

checks.q: Why is excess copper oxide added to the sulfuric acid?
checks.a: So that all the acid reacts (is neutralised) and no acid is left in the solution.

checks.q: How is the excess copper oxide removed from the mixture?
checks.a: Filter the mixture. The excess copper oxide stays on the filter paper and the copper sulfate solution is the filtrate.

checks.q: Potassium chloride is made from potassium hydroxide solution and hydrochloric acid. Why can you not just add excess potassium hydroxide and filter?
checks.a: Potassium hydroxide is soluble, so the excess cannot be filtered off. Titration is used to find the exact volumes, and the reaction is repeated without the indicator.

worked_example.question:
This question is about making a soluble salt.

Plan a method to make pure, dry crystals of zinc chloride from zinc carbonate and a dilute acid.
answer_points: Use zinc carbonate and hydrochloric acid. Add zinc carbonate to the acid in a beaker and stir.
Continue adding until the zinc carbonate is in excess, shown by excess solid and no more effervescence.
Filter the reaction mixture to remove the excess zinc carbonate.
Heat the solution, using a water bath or electric heater, to crystallisation point.
Pat the crystals dry with filter paper.
worked_example.tip: A six-mark plan is marked by level. The key steps must be in a logical order, with the correct chemicals chosen.

worked_example.question:
The word equation for the reaction between copper carbonate and dilute sulfuric acid is
copper carbonate + sulfuric acid → copper sulfate + carbon dioxide + water
Dilute sulfuric acid is in a conical flask.
Copper carbonate is added to the acid in the flask.
The copper carbonate is added one spatula measure at a time until the reaction has finished.

Describe how you would obtain a solution of copper sulfate from the mixture and how you would obtain pure, dry copper sulfate crystals from this solution.
Your description should include the apparatus you would use.
answer_points: Filter the mixture, using a filter funnel and filter paper, to remove the excess copper carbonate.
Collect the filtrate (copper sulfate solution) in a conical flask or other suitable container.
Pour it into an evaporating basin and heat on a water bath, or on a tripod over a Bunsen burner.
Heat until the solution is concentrated, or crystals start to appear around the edge.
Remove from the heat, cover with filter paper, allow to cool and crystallise.
Separate the crystals and dry them on filter paper in a warm place.
worked_example.tip: Level 3 needs a sequence including at least two of: filter, crystallise (heating and cooling), separate and dry.

worked_example.question:
Zinc nitrate can be made by reacting zinc oxide with nitric acid, HNO3.

Paul suggests this method for preparing zinc nitrate.

1. Measure 50cm3 of dilute nitric acid into a beaker.

2. Add one spatulaful of zinc oxide.

3. Heat the mixture until crystals of zinc nitrate are made.

Paul’s method will not make a pure dry sample of zinc nitrate.

What improvements should Paul make to the method to make sure that:

• the reaction is complete
• the zinc nitrate can be separated from the nitric acid and the zinc oxide?

Explain your answer.
answer_points: An excess of zinc oxide must be added.
So the reaction is complete, because all the nitric acid has reacted.
Filter off the excess zinc oxide.
Evaporate off some of the water, then allow the solution to crystallise.
worked_example.tip: Any four of five points score. Each improvement needs its reason.
